title: Maximum Width Ramp
description:
# Maximum Width Ramp

Given an integer array `nums`, a width ramp is a pair of indices `(i, j)` such that:

* `i < j`
* `nums[i] <= nums[j]`

The width of the ramp is `j - i`. Return the maximum width among all valid ramps. If no valid pair exists, return `0`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [6,0,8,2,1,5]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** The maximum width ramp is `(i, j) = (1, 5)` because `nums[1] = 0 <= 5 = nums[5]`, and `5 - 1 = 4`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [9,8,1,0,1,9,4,0,4,1]
**Output:** 7
**Explanation:** The maximum width ramp is `(2, 9)` because `nums[2] = 1 <= 1 = nums[9]`, and `9 - 2 = 7`.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 100000`
* `-1000000000 <= nums[i] <= 1000000000`
* Equal values are allowed in a ramp because the condition is `<=`, not `<`.

tests.description: Canonical ramp uses a low value near the front and a later larger value.
Wide ramp can begin at a small middle value and end near the back.
Already increasing array gives the full width from first to last index.
Strictly decreasing array has no valid ramp.
Equal values are allowed by the non-strict ramp condition.
Single element cannot form a pair, so the width is zero.
Negative values still follow normal numeric ordering.
The widest valid ramp can start at the first element when a later equal value exists.
A small middle value may form the best ramp even when the first value is too large.
The best ramp may span nearly the whole array despite noisy middle values.
Repeated low and high values should preserve the widest endpoint pair.

solutions.name: Monotonic Candidate Stack
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a stack of candidate left indices whose values are strictly decreasing as the indices move right. Then scan `j` from right to left. Whenever `nums[stackTop] <= nums[j]`, pop that left index and record the width.

## Key Insight

If an earlier index has a value no larger than a later candidate, the later candidate can never produce a wider ramp. The decreasing stack keeps only useful left endpoints, and scanning from the far right guarantees the first successful match for each popped index is its widest possible match.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Prefix Minimum and Suffix Maximum Two Pointers
solutions.description:
## Approach

Create `leftMin`, where `leftMin[i]` is the minimum value in `nums[0..i]`, and `rightMax`, where `rightMax[j]` is the maximum value in `nums[j..n-1]`. Then use two pointers `i` and `j`: if `leftMin[i] <= rightMax[j]`, a ramp of width `j - i` is possible, so move `j` right; otherwise move `i` right.

## Key Insight

For any left boundary `i`, only the smallest value seen up to `i` matters. For any right boundary `j`, only the largest value available from `j` onward matters. These two monotonic summaries make the width search a linear merge.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Sorted Indices Sweep
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort indices by `nums[index]`, breaking ties by index. Sweep that order from smallest value to largest value. For each current index, every previously seen index has a value no greater than the current value, so the best ramp ending here uses the smallest index seen so far.

## Key Insight

The condition `nums[i] <= nums[j]` becomes automatic once indices are processed in nondecreasing value order. The only remaining question is how far left the best compatible index can be.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Binary Search on Answer Width
solutions.description:
## Approach

Binary search the answer width. To test whether some ramp has width at least `w`, scan possible right endpoints `j >= w` while maintaining the minimum value among indices `0..j-w`. If that minimum is at most `nums[j]`, a ramp of width at least `w` exists.

## Key Insight

The predicate “there exists a ramp of width at least `w`” is monotonic. If a large width works, every smaller width works; if a width fails, every larger width fails. The feasibility scan must check width at least `w`, not exactly `w`.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Brute Force Pair Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach

Check every pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`. Whenever `nums[i] <= nums[j]`, update the best width. This directly implements the definition of a ramp.

## Key Insight

The brute force method is too slow for the full constraint size, but it is the clearest correctness baseline: every optimized method must produce the same maximum over exactly these valid pairs.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
